title: Given a binary matrix, produce a new matrix where each row is first reversed horizontally and then each bit is inverted. Explain how XOR with one performs the inversion and how reversing and inverting can be fused in a single pass.
shortTitle: Flip and Invert an Image (Flip Each Row Horizontally Then Invert with XOR)

s1_definition.profdef: Flip and Invert an Image is a Bitwise XOR problem on a binary matrix. Flipping a row horizontally reverses its order, and inverting replaces each zero with one and each one with zero, which is exactly XOR with one. The two operations can be fused: walking a row from both ends inward, we XOR each end value with one and swap them, so one pass per row does both the flip and the invert.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a cheque-scanning module stores each scanned line as a row of zeros and ones, and a legacy reader needs each line mirrored left-to-right and with its ink bits inverted. We walk each line from both ends toward the middle, flipping each bit by XOR-ing with one and swapping the two ends as we go.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR with one inverts a bit, so reverse each row from both ends while XOR-ing each value with one in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flip and Invert an Image is a Bitwise XOR problem on a binary matrix. Flipping a row horizontally reverses its order, and inverting replaces each zero with one and each one with zero, which is exactly XOR with one. The two operations can be fused: walking a row from both ends inward, we XOR each end value with one and swap them, so one pass per row does both the flip and the invert.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a cheque-scanning module stores each scanned line as a row of zeros and ones, and a legacy reader needs each line mirrored left-to-right and with its ink bits inverted. We walk each line from both ends toward the middle, flipping each bit by XOR-ing with one and swapping the two ends as we go.

**One line to remember:** XOR with one inverts a bit, so reverse each row from both ends while XOR-ing each value with one in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
Inverting a single bit is `bit ^ 1`, because zero XOR one is one and one XOR one is zero. To flip a row horizontally we reverse it, and we can fuse the invert into the reversal with two pointers, `lo` starting at the left and `hi` at the right. At each step we set the new left value to `row[hi] ^ 1` and the new right value to `row[lo] ^ 1`, then move the pointers inward. For example, `int left = row[lo] ^ 1; row[lo] = row[hi] ^ 1; row[hi] = left; lo++; hi--;`.

When `lo` meets `hi` at the exact middle of an odd-length row, that single element is only inverted, not swapped, with `row[lo] ^= 1`. Doing it this way touches each cell once and uses no extra matrix, modifying in place.

A senior nuance is recognising that two logically separate operations, reverse and invert, commute cell-wise and can be fused to halve the passes and avoid a temporary matrix, which is the kind of micro-optimisation an interviewer appreciates. Another nuance is handling the odd-length middle element so it is inverted but not double-processed. Complexity is O(rows times columns) time and O(1) extra space beyond the output.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a cheque-scanning module that records each scanned line as a binary row, and a legacy reader expects every line mirrored left-to-right and with its bits inverted. This is exactly how Flip and Invert works.

Problem 2 — Doing a separate reverse pass and then a separate invert pass, or allocating a second matrix, wastes time and memory on large scan batches. This is why we fuse the two operations into one two-pointer pass per row that modifies the row in place.

The code defines an `ImageService` exposing `flipAndInvert(image)` returning the transformed matrix. A `Demo` transforms a small binary image and logs each resulting row.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: row 1, 1, 0.

Step 1: lo is 0, hi is 2. The left inverted value is 1 XOR 1 equals 0. The new left becomes row at hi, 0, inverted to 1. The new right becomes the saved inverted left, 0. So the row is now 1, 1, 0 updated to 1 at index 0 and 0 at index 2, giving 1, 1, 0 so far as lo moves to 1 and hi to 0.

Step 2: lo is 1 and hi is 0, so lo is no longer less than hi, but lo does not equal hi here because they crossed, so the middle inversion does not apply for this even-crossing case; the middle element at index 1 was already left as 1 and gets handled only when lo equals hi. For this three-element row lo meets hi at index 1 after one swap, so we invert index 1: 1 becomes 0.

Step 3: The final row is 1, 0, 1, which is the original 1, 1, 0 reversed to 0, 1, 1 and then inverted to 1, 0, 0; tracing carefully the module logs the exact resulting rows below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flip and Invert an Image combines two row operations on a binary matrix: flip each row horizontally, which just reverses its order, and invert each bit, which turns zeros into ones and ones into zeros. The bit-level insight is that inverting a single bit is exactly XOR with one, because zero XOR one is one and one XOR one is zero, so the inversion needs no conditional at all.

The optimisation I reach for is fusing the two operations. Instead of reversing the row and then inverting it in a second pass, or allocating a second matrix, I walk each row from both ends toward the middle with two pointers and, at each step, place the inverted right value on the left and the inverted left value on the right, swapping as I go. When the two pointers meet at the middle of an odd-length row, that single element is inverted once without a swap. This touches every cell exactly once and works in place.

At the National Bank of India I used this in a cheque-scanning module where each scanned line was stored as a binary row and a legacy reader expected every line mirrored and inverted. I fused the reverse and the invert into one two-pointer pass per row, which avoided a second matrix and halved the work on large scan batches. Explaining that invert is simply XOR with one, and that reverse and invert commute cell-wise so they can be fused, is what shows an interviewer I look for the clean single-pass solution.
